name: SHU-9119
lead: SHU-9119 (also written SHU9119) is a laboratory melanocortin receptor antagonist used in animal research on appetite and energy balance. [1] Studies in rats infused it into the brain's third ventricle as a tool to block melanocortin signaling, alongside the agonist alpha-MSH. [1]
It is not a drug approved for humans, and no human clinical studies were found. It is a research peptide whose effects in animals include increased feeding and altered insulin action. [1]

paras: A 2001 study reported that week-long infusions of SHU9119 into the third cerebral ventricle of rats affected insulin action and the body distribution of fat, in contrast with the agonist alpha-MSH. [1] The compound sits within wider work on the melanocortin system, including the 1997 Nature paper on agouti and melanocortin neurons in feeding, studies of agouti-related protein as an antagonist or inverse agonist at MC4R, and brainstem applications of melanocortin ligands. [2][3][4][5][6]
Other animal work used melanocortin blockade in a rat model of cancer anorexia. [7]
No studies found. Research is in animals: rodent studies of the melanocortin pathway are cited above. [1][2][6][7]

card.summary: Lab melanocortin antagonist used in rodent appetite research; no human studies and no approved use.

quick.overview:
SHU-9119 is a research peptide that blocks melanocortin receptors. Scientists have used it in rats to study appetite, body weight and insulin action.

It has no approved use and no human trials were found.
quick.mechanism: It antagonizes melanocortin receptors (MC3R and MC4R) in the brain, opposing the signal of alpha-MSH.
quick.risks: No human safety data exist; in animals, blocking this pathway increased feeding.
